articles.title: AI Destruction Isn’t Hypothetical. It’s Already Here.
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: We’re several weeks into a fierce debate over whether artificial intelligence (AI) will kill us all. Triggered by a spate of former workers at major AI firms coming forward to warn that a future superintelligent AI could lead to human extinction, the debate has inspired a kaleidoscopic array of views that don’t break down along neat ideological lines. Some think it’s all hogwash, either the product of ignorant hype or part of a cynical hype campaign by the industry itself. For others, convinced that the tech’s potential capabilities are no joke, they’re warnings that need to be taken deadly seriously.In many ways, though, the debate is besides the point. It’s not that we shouldn’t try to get to the bottom of what exactly happened with the HuggingFace hacking incident, and that we shouldn’t worry about the question of rogue agents or the dangers of a future superintelligent AI that could threaten our continued existence. It’s that what we call AI has already copiously proven it carries profound danger for the human race — and is doing immense harm way before it’s even remotely close to reaching superintelligence.Consider the fact that AI “almost started a war” between the United States and China this past spring, in the words of one source who told CNN about it. A special operations command analyst had used a chatbot to put together a report about the cargo of a Chinese ship sailing in the Middle East, which hallucinated that the vessel was carrying the components of a nuclear weapons program, prompting the US military to mobilize to intercept and board the ship, guns drawn. Military planes had even taken off for this purpose. The operation was called off after officials looked into the report and realized it was AI-generated nonsense.According to CNN, the incident was the result of two overlapping trends: the fact that younger “AI native” analysts tend to rely on and trust the technology to an inordinate degree and the Pentagon’s aggressive adoption of AI under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It’s worth noting that if any direct war were to break out between the United States and China, it would carry grave danger for the entire world, not just because it would likely lead to a global depression, but because any military hostilities between the two have a high chance of going nuclear — something that really could threaten the survival of our species.The incident perfectly distills the very real, currently existing dangers of AI. We’re so fixated on the future catastrophic potential of hypothetical superintelligent AI agents that we’re forgetting AI is already causing real harm and carrying massive risks — not because it’s smarter than us, but because it is flawed, error-ridden technology that we are rushing to shoehorn into seemingly every facet of our lives.That includes war. Long before the incident with the Chinese ship, AI was directly responsible for the horrific, mass loss of innocent human life thanks to being folded into military operations. We saw it most recently with the Trump administration’s murder of scores of Iranian schoolgirls, where the military’s trust in Palantir’s AI tool Maven was a major part of the chain of disastrous decision-making that led to the atrocity.US Central Command personnel reportedly compressed what used to be hours of work involved in choosing targets into a few minutes by feeding the underlying intelligence into Maven, simply assuming the AI tool would catch and highlight any errors. It did not. Before that, we saw AI used in a more apocalyptic way for the purpose of war in Gaza, where AI targeting was at the heart of Israel’s indisciminate flattening of the territory.But this is only the most overtly homicidal use of AI. Many of its social harms have been more insidious.The unleashing of AI onto the public has caused a by now widely documented phenomenon of what Massachusettes Institute of Technology researchers have termed “cognitive surrender” among college students who, struggling with deadlines and the pressure to succeed, have turned en masse to using the technology to write their essays and otherwise do assignments for them. The proportion of students doing this has now reached a depressing 95 percent.The outsourcing of their very thinking to machines has meant that young graduates are not just emerging from their studies without seemingly actually learning their field but with genuinely weaker brain power: a worse memory, an inability to persist with intellectual challenges, and vanishing critical thinking skills. Wall Street firms, normally big boosters of the AI industry, have, when push comes to shove, found themselves less than impressed with the young workers it is producing, underwhelmed at a generation of new hires who prove remarkably shallow thinkers. It’s so bad that the students themselves think the technology is weakening their critical thinking even as they continue to rely on it.Meanwhile, as people have turned to AI for therapy and other help with their personal demons, AI chatbots have been linked to a series of suicides and even murders by troubled individuals, a number of them teenagers. The problem is that the technology — besides not being human or having professional mental health expertise — is designed to flatter, please, and otherwise keep the user engaged as long as possible. As a result, chatbots’ role in these tragedies has ranged from being useless to help users, to feeding their delusions and actively helping them hurt themselves or others.That’s when AI isn’t helping otherwise mentally stable individuals hurt themselves with lethally bad advice: the man hospitalized after ChatGPT likely advised him to replace salt in his diet with an old-fashioned sedative; the stranded hikers who nearly died when Google Gemini advised them to pack far less food and water than they needed; the pastor who nearly died of a pulmonary embolism after ChatGPT advised him not to seek medical help; the elderly neuroscientist who put off cancer treatment because he had come to trust AI hallucinations over his own doctor; and so many more.This is because AI chatbots and other tools often do not know what they’re talking about. One study (from an AI provider, no less) found seventeen large language models (LLMs) only answered two out of five financial questions correctly. Another found they hallucinate legal responses between 58 and 88 percent of the time.AI chatbots sycophantically back a variety of potentially harmful statements from users nearly half (47 percent) of the time, according to another. This is particularly alarming when it comes to medical advice, which a study found AI was accurate about only 76 percent of the time — a passing grade for a college paper but abysmal in the medical context, where being wrong once could mean death or debilitation.But it’s not just chatbots. AI’s rapid integration into a variety of expert fields has led to adverse consequences. Court sanctions are on the rise because lawyers keep filing briefs with AI-made errors. On the other side of the bench, two federal judges allegedly relied on AI to issue error-ridden court orders, a serious concern given the expansive power courts have in the US political system, and because judges are broadly insulated from civil liability. The use of AI for medical devices used in surgeries has caused a spate of injuries, including strokes after surgeons were misdirected by the technology in ways that damaged arteries.A Stanford and Harvard study from earlier this year found the best AI models made “severely harmful clinical recommendations” in medical cases 22 percent of the time, often through omission. In other cases, AI is being used by doctor’s and dentist’s offices to justify hawking expensive treatments that patients don’t actually need.And then there is the way that AI algorithms are being used to exacerbate and justify preexisting corporate malfeasance. An ongoing class-action lawsuit against UnitedHealth alleges that its various companies used an error-prone AI tool to serially deny insurance to patients. A different lawsuit alleges that an AI recruiting software carried out systematic employment discrimination against black applicants and others.In all of these cases, people are being hurt or threatened by AI not because it’s achieved sentience and is smarter than us, but the opposite: because it’s a flawed, at times comically inept technology that humans are actively making choices to deploy in situations where it is most likely to do serious damage, sometimes in ways actively designed to screw over others.In fact, it is arguably the very market-driven hype about AI’s imminent superintelligence that has contributed to all this. Overstating AI’s capabilities has helped encourage its rapid uptake in fields like war or health care depite the fact that it’s not ready for prime time and makes those unfamiliar with or ignorant about the technology more likely to take what it says at face value, even when it’s wrong or hallucinating.The dangers of a hypothetical AI superintelligence should be a concern. But we do not have to determine if this is really our future to be able to call for development of this technology to be urgently paused, for it to be heavily regulated, and to put serious guardrails on it, if not outright banish it from being used for particular purposes. The dumber, mistake-prone AI of today is enough of a risk to humanity as it is.

articles.title: Francis Fukuyama Is Welcoming History Back
articles.author: Matt McManus
articles.content: In his new autobiography, Francis Fukuyama boasts that for decades “students in introductory classes in international relations all over the world were required to read [Samuel Huntington’s The Clash of Civilizations ] alongside The End of History .” The flex is warranted; during my undergrad we were assigned both essays in one of my classes on international law. Many intellectuals dream about reaching this level of notoriety. But for Fukuyama, fame came at a heavy price. Namely, he became the kind of thinker whose ideas everyone has an opinion on even while they resolutely avoid reading him (see 99 percent of recent conservative commentary on Karl Marx and Marxism for an example). For years, Fukuyama’s problematic but provocative thesis about reaching the “end of history” was subjected to a lot of superficial criticism from the Left and the Right. A standard move by critical intellectuals was to hold Fukuyama up as the poster boy for smug triumphalist neoliberalism, resting thoughtlessly on its post–Cold War laurels. This was true even if, as Slavoj Žižek often points out , in practice most leftist intellectuals and parties seem to have accepted the inevitability of capitalist realism. On the other side of the fence, right-wing critics like Huntington chastised Fukuyama with a kind of squishy liberal optimism, hypothesizing that humanity wasn’t quite done clashing with itself yet. A Portrait of the Last Man as a Young Man In the Realm of the Last Man is an unusual book; an autobiography that pulls triple duty, it ruminates on its subject’s complex life, sets the record straight on past debates and criticisms, and closes by defending liberal democracy against rising competitors on the Left and Right. The book pulls off the first two admirably, though the apologia for liberal democracy highlights some of Fukuyama’s limitations as a commentator. The self-portrait Fukuyama paints is of an intellectually inclined man who has always tempered his speculative impulses while keeping one foot firmly on the ground. Aside from giving himself the occasional and by and large justified pats on the back, Fukuyama comes across as a confident but relatively humble man well aware of what he owes to others. The long sections on how his ethnically Japanese family was interred in concentration camps during World War II are filled with righteous indignation. Honestly describing his complex relationship with his professor father, Fukuyama notes how he “remained a diehard liberal his whole life.” The elder Fukuyama was disappointed when his son gravitated toward moderate conservatism. This rightward shift “pained my father greatly”, we are told. “He didn’t really understand what had changed my thinking; he told his friends that one of my professors had gone to work for the Pentagon and ‘brainwashed’ me after returning to academia.” Fukuyama admits to regretting some of this youthful animosity toward his father and ending up now committed to the kind of progressive liberalism he dismissed as a young man. This transition from left to center-right to center-left critic of radicalism on either side takes up the bulk of Fukuyama’s reflections. Early on, he became fascinated with postmodern critical theories of Michel Foucault, Jacques Derrida, and other French philosophers. These were all the rage in the 1970s, and Fukuyama recounts that his “fascination with postmodernism led me to graduate from Cornell early and move to Paris so I could study with the masters.” Unfortunately, this exposure to unfiltered postmodern theory led him to conclude that these ideas were part of a project that was “essentially nihilistic, built on the assertions of the impossibility of reasoned discourse, inference from empirical evidence, and ultimately of philosophy itself. Truth claims simply masked the assertions of power by a dominant social actor at the expense of groups that were marginalized.” The Burdens of History Frustrated by postmodernism’s endless criticism, Fukuyama chose to move in the opposite direction. Before graduating he fell under the influence of Alexandre Kojève, Allan Bloom, and Leo Strauss, among others. Though they differed substantially in their theoretical and political beliefs, they were united in their conviction that philosophy’s pursuit of capital T truth was a noble enterprise. Of particular importance to Fukuyama was the debate between Leo Strauss and the Hegelian philosopher Alexandre Kojève. In Natural Right and History , Strauss famously repudiated the strong versions of historicism — the view that social values and institutions were entirely the product of historical developments rather than human nature — associated with Edmund Burke, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, and Karl Marx. Whether in its more conservative or radical forms, historicism led to the view that what counted as true and good was largely settled by the norms of the time. Strauss was famously guarded about his own philosophical preferences but expressed a qualified admiration for the commitment to discovering timeless truths one saw in ancient philosophy. Kojève, however, famously interpreted Hegel as arguing that human nature developed over time, and with it our ability to more richly understand our relation to truth and to one another. Consequently, the philosopher’s goal wasn’t to understand transcendent truths but rather the process of how our conceptions of truth became richer over time. Kojève gave this idea a political spin, hypothesizing that one day we would reach the “end of history”; there would be no more debates worth having because we will have worked out how to offer meaningful recognition to each and all. Fukuyama describes his own view as “middle ground between the Strauss and Kojève positions, and indeed the middle ground is what I tried to elaborate in The End of History and the Last Man.” He is sympathetic to the view that historical processes shape human convictions, and that changes in politics and society are possible. This includes the prospect of improvement through the cautious application of reason; most radically, this increasingly includes the ability to apply science to alter major features of human biology even prior to conception. The prospect of endless unconstrained change worries Fukuyama, who insists that there is such a thing as human nature. What he means by this is a “core set of faculties and inclinations that ultimately served to limit human autonomy and ensure that there was also continuity in the human experience over time.” One of these core human inclinations is what he, drawing on ancient Greek philosophy, calls the thymotic desire for recognition. In his book Identity , Fukuyama describes thymos as the “third part of the soul” alongside desire and reason. Thymos is “the seat of judgements of worth. . . . [individuals driven by thymos] also crave positive judgements about their worth or dignity. Those judgements can come from within. . . . but they are most often made by other people in the society around them who recognize their worth.” Fukuyama thinks that while liberal societies have done much to rationally organize societies to secure many human needs, they have long struggled to offer anything like equal recognition to all their members. This stirs the thymotic yearnings of the soul, leading to resentment of those who are recognized as greater or more valuable. Fukuyama is not usually understood as a thinker interested in human psychology, but this is more a product of a general failure to read more than the title of The End of History and the Last Man . Few familiar with this work ever “ bothered to read the last five chapters of my book, which dealt with the problem of the last man.” The book is a considered rumination on whether liberal capitalism was indeed the last ideology standing at the end of history. At the time Fukuyama hypothesized it might be, left-wing alternatives to liberal capitalism were lifeless — the Soviet Union was still tottering on in 1989 when Fukuyama wrote the essay, “The End of History?”, on which he based his book, but it collapsed two years later, as if to promote his hardcover. The fall of the Soviet Union profoundly discredited communism, while many of the Left’s brightest minds had become enamored with trendy but ultimately “nihilistic” postmodern critical theory of which Fukuyama had always been wary. Drawing on Friedrich Nietzsche, the last chapters of The End of History make the case that many right-of-center personalities will remain driven by “megalothymonia” — a yearning for a sense of superiority and greatness that makes them discontented with merely being the well-paid but bored technocratic managers of docile nations and respectably successful companies. As he put it near the close of The End of History : It is reasonable to wonder whether all people will believe that the kinds of struggles and sacrifices possible in a self-satisfied and prosperous liberal democracy are sufficient to call forth what is highest in man. For are there not indeed reservoirs of idealism that cannot be exhausted — indeed, that are not even touched — if one becomes a developer like Donald Trump, or a mountain climber like Reinhold Messner, or a politician like George Bush? Difficult as it is, in many ways, to be these individuals, and for all the recognition that they receive, their lives are not the most difficult, and the causes they serve are not the most serious or the most just. And as long as they are not, the horizon of human possibilities that they define will not be ultimately satisfying for the most thymotic natures. Fukuyama remains committed in broad strokes to the story he told more than thirty years ago. Liberal democracy provided material affluence and rational government for many. But personalities like Trump did indeed find simply being real estate developers and New York playboys destined for an esteemed place in the Epstein files unsatisfying. They wanted to be Alexandrian men of destiny, but they could only do this by smashing the liberal order and replacing it with one of their own making. Fukuyama shows real insight into the enduring populist appeal of the Right when he notes that liberals failed to recognize how these prejudices concealed a yearning to make moral judgements about the world that were more forceful than what mere toleration seemed to allow. In addition to failing to address the emotional needs of those who had no interest in just being an equal citizen in a society of equal citizens, liberalism failed to recognize the need people have for meaning beyond living day-to-day. These dissatisfied constituencies were primed to listen to megalothymotically driven populists who stoked their anger at being looked down upon by self-righteous liberals that chastised their moral views as so many racist, sexist, homophobic, and nationalist prejudices. What Trump et al. offered them was confirmation of their own moral superiority over those who pretended to be their betters, alongside a sense of cosmic significance in combating the evils of a decaying elite liberal order. For Fukuyama, the January 6 protesters didn’t just riot because they thought the election had been stolen from them. They wanted to “play-act at being armed revolutionaries defending their way of life” against sinister globalists and immigrant baristas making $7.50 an hour alike. The reality was that “they were simply dupes enlisted to soothe the ego of a single narcissistic fraudster.” Liberalism After History Restarted The end of history ended after about twenty-five years, give or take, and we are very much in an era in which liberal democracy faces pressure on all fronts. Fukuyama has deep insights into the roots of the attack from the Right, which makes a great deal of sense given his early attraction to Strauss, Bloom, and the neoconservative movement — although his understanding of the Left’s impulses is more questionable. Throughout In The Realm of the Last Man he expresses considerable regret for where this early attraction led him. He signed a periodical calling for the United States to invade Iraq and unseat Saddam Hussein in the late 1990s. This of course ended in the death of almost a million Iraqi people and thousands of Americans troops. Fukuyama admits that he was driven to sign the letter more out of group loyalty than hawkishness. “The problem was psychological, and not a matter of policy judgement or moral disagreement. The issue was a mental block against taking a public stand against the views of longtime friends.” When Fukuyama did eventually break with the neoconservatives, it came at a significant cost, though he admits it was “liberating” to abandon right-wing orthodoxy and adopt more social democratic positions. Despite Fukuyama’s journey of maturation to the social democratic left, he still struggles with understanding the instincts and ideas that animate it. His curt dismissal of complex thinkers like Foucault and Derrida is just the tip of the iceberg. Fukuyama rather lazily dismisses the students who set up pro-Palestinian encampments as privileged ne’er-do-wells who “want a break from their lives of steady and unheroic striving” and quips that they are not “similarly outraged at the situation of Ukrainians besieged by Russia or victims of the civil war in Sudan.” The difference — that America’s government isn’t allied to Russia or Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces but is deeply committed to supporting Israel — seems not to register to Fukuyama. Elsewhere in In the Realm of the Last Man , Fukuyama complains that there is “no clear systematic vision on the left for what kind of society should replace liberal democracy, as there once was.” He is deeply wary of the recent tendency of young people to become “more sympathetic to socialism or Communism than previously” since in the past these have led to “nightmares.” This take is wildly out of date. Proposals for everything from “ Nordic socialism ” to “ socialism in the twenty-first century ” to “ liberal socialism ” abound. Moreover, these didn’t come out of a vacuum. Any decent history of socialism would show it is a political and economic tradition that’s as internally diverse as liberalism and conservatism are. A general refusal to draw too deeply on left-wing insights limits major dimensions of Fukuyama’s diagnosis of liberalism’s woes. He’s absolutely correct that the Right has always had a significant constituency made up of people who are dissatisfied with the prospect of being their brother’s equal and keeper. They want to conceive of themselves, and be acknowledged as, “recognizable superiors”, as Friedrich Hayek noted in his thoughtful essay “Why I Am Not A Conservative.” Many of the resentments that appear on the Right are fueled by anxiety around dispossession; that the unworthy, unwashed multitudes of the world are threatening to take away the hard-earned riches of citizens or positions at Ivy League universities. This combination of believing oneself to be simultaneously a superior and also a victim of the weak is very powerful and has given the Right a lot of cultural pull. But Fukuyama’s book doesn’t sufficiently interrogate the social origins of these attitudes, perhaps because its author remains at least somewhat sympathetic to them. He often chimes in to acclaim the importance of meritocracy and even gives one cheer for megalothymia as a “necessary motivator of any kind of human excellence. . . . ” What this doesn’t interrogate is just how the very emphasis liberals place on meritocratic mythologies has contributed to festering social resentments. Given his stated admiration for Michael Sandel, Fukuyama might have engaged with the former’s important book The Tyranny of Merit . Sandel is very critical of how the meritocratic myth that everyone ought to be given a (very unequal) opportunity to succeed while acknowledging that most will not succeed has produced pathological results. We have a vulgar ruling class that increasingly tells itself it owes nothing to anyone, and worse, many poor and lower-middle-class people who are told that if they can’t make it they have no one to blame but themselves. The message for the poor under meritocratic liberal capitalism is simple: save your pennies, cut out the Budweiser, and either go to college or invest early in Bitcoin. It should come as no surprise that a society riven by such toxic ideas would generate mass forms of resentment, and much of the blame must be laid at the feet of liberals who propagated meritocratic mythologies even in the face of mounting evidence showing the immeasurable amount we owe to others for whatever success we are lucky enough to achieve. At the conclusion of the 1989 essay, Fukuyama admitted he could “feel in myself, and see in others around me, a powerful nostalgia for the time when history existed”. Now history is once again back, the older Fukuyama mainly seems to feel a powerful nostalgia for the post-historical 1990s. He should be careful what he wishes for. It is perhaps appropriate that he would remain, to the last, someone whose political allegiances are stamped by the ideological parameters established back when neoliberal hegemony seemed untouchable. Over time, Fukuyama has steadily moved from the neoliberalism and neoconservatism of Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush to the moderate progressivism of Bill Clinton and Joe Biden. But it was the failure of just these forms of centrism that paved the road to Trumpism — and they will not save us from it.

articles.title: Cuba Under Siege
articles.content: A ​ “ silent Gaza.” That is how a Cuban citizen summed up the impact of the U.S. decades-long blockade that the Trump administration has aggressively ratcheted up since the beginning of the year. In January, weeks after the military assault on Venezuela and the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro, Trump, invoking a ​ “ national emergency,” signed an executive order establishing punitive tariffs against any country that would provide Cuba with oil. Cuba depended on Venezuela for the largest share of its energy needs, in an ​ “ oil-for-doctors” agreement established in 2000 by Hugo Chávez and Fidel Castro. The country received 100 , 000 barrels of oil per day in exchange for tens of thousands of Cuban doctors, sports trainers and other professionals who provided Venezuelans with care and technical assistance — an extension of the medical internationalism that has long been a hallmark of the socialist island state. The policy of what UN experts have called ​ “ energy starvation” is wreaking devastation on its public health system, affecting crucial medicines, medical device components and, above all, the fuel required to power hospital facilities. Health workers have had to manually ventilate newborns by squeezing air into their breathing tubes as they wait for backup generators to start functioning during power outages. As public health scholar Arachu Castro has analyzed in a Think Global Health piece, the United States’ fuel blockade, combined with its punitive restrictions on other countries seeking to provide Cuba with humanitarian assistance, has generated a ​ “ polycrisis,” in which the deliberate deprivation of fuel is ​ “ producing cascading harm across every health domain.” The fuel shortages have stopped imports of crucial medicines by air and sea, stranded humanitarian aid at ports and impeded refrigerated transport of vaccines and other vital materials. Any import substitution has also been rendered impossible by the systematic policy of energy starvation. As Castro concludes: ​ “ The longer the convergence of fuel shortages, pharmaceutical inaccessibility and technological deterioration persists, the less reversible the damage becomes — particularly for patients whose treatment windows close.” Misnamed an ​ “ embargo” — which suggests a government’s decision to unilaterally suspend trade with another state — the intensifying blockade of Cuba is a paradigmatic instance of economic warfare, which employs U.S. geopolitical clout along with extraterritorial financial and legal blackmail to prevent third countries from alleviating Cuba’s plight. Human rights experts appointed by the UN Human Rights Council declared in June that American ​ “ efforts to change the constitutional order of a sovereign State through threats and coercion echo colonial-era practices.” Like the Israeli siege that suffocated Gaza before and since the beginning of the genocide, the blockade of Cuba reveals the racist and genocidal logic at work in colonial and imperial sieges. And Trump recently announced ​ “ economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale” against the Islamic Republic of Iran. These sieges grimly exemplify abolitionist geographer Ruth Wilson Gilmore’s oft-cited definition of racism as ​ “ the state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death.” The production and exploitation of the vulnerabilities of the Cuban population with lethal intent were envisaged even before John F. Kennedy issued a presidential proclamation stopping all trade with Cuba in February 1962 . In a secret memo penned in April 1960 , Eisenhower’s Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs, Lester D. Mallory, exploring strategies to crush a socialist revolution 90 miles away from the Florida coastline, proposed that — given majority support for Fidel Castro — the only way ​ “ of alienating internal support is through disenchantment and disaffection based on economic dissatisfaction and hardship.” To that end, ​ “ every possible means should be undertaken promptly to weaken the economic life of Cuba … denying money and supplies to Cuba, to decrease monetary and real wages, to bring about hunger, desperation and overthrow of government.” With the partial exception of the brief period of normalization at the tail end of the presidency of Barack Obama, Mallory’s philosophy has defined the United States’ relentless and still unsuccessful drive to bring Cuba to heel. As economist Helen Yaffe has compellingly argued, the Cuba blockade is ​ “ the longest and most comprehensive set of sanctions in modern history,” ​ “ a key instrument in the U.S. toolkit to pursue regime change on the island,” ​ “ an act of war” and ​ “ a violation of human rights designed to obstruct Cuban development” — together with any idea of a socialist alternative. The United States has exercised its imperial prerogative as capitalist hegemon to exert extraterritorial control over Cuba’s ability to survive — imposing punitive sanctions on foreign entities, including European banks, willing to transact with Cuba and preventing it from accessing any financial lifelines. The energy starvation is underwritten by a legal and financial siege, and the impact is brutal: Cuban economists have estimated the cost of the blockade to the island’s economy at $ 4 . 4 billion annually. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have built on the legal, political and ideological infrastructure of over six decades of economic warfare against Cuba with the widely advertised aim of bringing the Cuban state to breaking point. While continuities with the past should not be downplayed, it is also important to understand the novelty of the present moment. The ratcheting up of the siege on Cuba is part of a bullish turn to the Americas as the arena for the unrivaled projection of U.S. power. This hemispheric pivot has taken place under the cringeworthy banner of the ​ “ Donroe Doctrine,” as laid out in the 2025 National Security Strategy and incessantly trumpeted by U.S. officials — from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s call to ​ “ Make the Americas Great Again” to U.S. Ambassador to Panama Kevin Marino Cabrera’s video promoting the virtues of unchecked U.S. regional supremacy. This pivot is by no means all bluster. The Trump administration has been disturbingly successful in its efforts to promote a surge in the electoral fortunes of the far right across the Americas. A kind of ​ “ Alliance for Regression” ranges from Javier Milei in Argentina to Nayib Bukele in El Salvador to Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia to José Antonio Kast in Chile. Brought together under the aegis of the Shield of the Americas under the threadbare pretext of a war on ​ “ narco-terrorists,” this consolidating network of alliances is aimed at turning the Western Hemisphere from the ​ “ backyard” of the U.S. superpower to what William Callison and Verónica Gago have termed ​ “ a frontyard of fascist experimentation.” While electoral autocracy seems to be the preferred method, the Trump administration is happy to revive the belligerent model of Grenada’s 1983 invasion or Panama’s in 1989 . In an operation that was also clearly intended to open up the Cuban front, the abduction of Maduro gave way to the capture and remote control of Delcy Rodríguez’s government in Venezuela, with Marco Rubio reported to be co-running the country via WhatsApp and with the critical oil sector in U.S. hands and the Venezuelan state subordinating its foreign policy to U.S. diktats. Trump was so taken with the spectacle of this Venezuelan model’s success— what has come to be termed ​ “ regime management” or ​ “ regime editing” — that he rather absurdly imagined it could be applied to Iran (even demanding he be allowed to name the new Ayatollah while the Israelis conspired to anoint famous anti-Semite Mahmoud Ahmadinejad). No secret has been made of the wish to apply this model to Cuba as well, with much talk that the siege might be lifted if the Cuban president Miguel DíazCanel could be replaced. To this end, a new CIA task force has been set up to create divisions among the governing elite. The candidate for Trump’s man in Havana appears to be Raúl G. Rodríguez Castro— grandson of Cuba’s former leader, the 95 -year-old Raúl Castro, who the United States indicted on murder charges in May. Rodríguez Castro already met with John Ratcliffe during the CIA director’s visit to Cuba and was recently interviewed by USA Today , declaring (even though on paper he is merely a colonel in the Ministry of the Interior and holds no official position) that he is open to negotiating with Trump himself. The notion that diplomacy and legality can be jettisoned for the sake of personalized ​ “ deals” with the true wielders of power, so characteristic of Trump and his entourage, is yet again on show. Capitalism — not the implementation of a market system as much as the possibility for unbridled plunder and gain for those aligned with the Trump administration — is at the heart of the siege, which operates as a tool of imperial extortion. The blockade has already resulted in a raft of economic measures implemented by Díaz-Canel’s government that would open up the island to capital and real estate investments, especially from a diasporic Cuban-American business class set on the overthrow of Communist Party rule. Trump has made no secret that he would like to build the first hotel after the fall of castrismo . It doesn’t seem a stretch to suggest that Cuba before the revolution, the kind of paradise of plunder depicted in The Godfather Part II , is as close to Trump’s utopia as one could imagine.

articles.title: Immigrants Aren't Taking Away Our Healthcare—ICE Is
articles.content: The cost of healthcare just keeps going up — and millions of Americans are set to lose coverage. Under the GOP’s so-called ​ “ Big Beautiful Bill,” around 17 million people in this country will lose health care thanks to the law’s Medicaid cuts, failure to renew Affordable Care Act subsidies and other changes. Those cuts accelerate after this year’s midterms. Instead, that money is going toward tax cuts for the rich plus record budgets for Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Pentagon. Immigrants — including well over 1 million residents who are lawfully present — will be especially hard hit. Rosa Maria Carranza fled El Salvador’s civil war for the United States decades ago, working here and sending money home to support her three children. She missed their milestones as she worked overnight shifts babysitting and substitute-teaching. Later, she co-founded a preschool. Now semi-retired and working part-time, her livelihood depends on the Medicare and Social Security benefits she earned by paying taxes into the system for decades. Yet Carranza is now expected to lose Medicare coverage, according to KFF Health News . Carranza is just one of the 100 , 000 lawfully present immigrants who are expected to be cut out of Medicare — and one of 1 . 4 million projected to lose their healthcare overall from other changes under the law, the Kaiser Family Foundation calculates. Meanwhile, intensified ICE raids have led many immigrants to avoid getting care for fear of being detained by ICE. President Trump and many other MAGA Republicans tried to justify these deep healthcare cuts by accusing immigrants of taking care away from citizens. This is a lie — instead, millions of citizens are losing their own healthcare in part to fund ICE’s crackdown on immigrants. Undocumented immigrants are not allowed to enroll for Medicaid and Medicare, and they’re ineligible to purchase health care through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace. Even before the Big Beautiful Bill, immigrants needed to have a ​ “ qualified” immigration status to be eligible for Medicaid — and most would still have to wait five years after gaining qualified status to enroll. While lawfully present immigrants can also qualify for Medicare, they first must have ​ “ sufficient” work history. As a result of factors like these, lawfully present immigrants are more than three times as likely as U.S. citizens to be uninsured. And both lawfully present and undocumented immigrants use less healthcare due to higher uninsured rates, language barriers, and fear of ICE . The Big Beautiful Bill will make this worse. The law restricts the definition of qualified immigrants who are eligible for Medicaid as well as Medicare, excluding legally present refugees, asylum seekers, immigrants on certain work visas, and others. And of course that’s alongside deep cuts to Medicaid itself that will cause millions of citizens to lose their coverage as well. Even while immigrants are losing healthcare coverage, they continue to pay billions into the system. In 2022 , immigrants paid $ 579 billion in taxes — including $ 96 . 7 billion from undocumented immigrants. Moreover, since immigrants are more likely to work in physically demanding jobs with lower wages and weaker benefits, they may have a greater need for the care they’re being systematically denied. Cracking down on immigrants was never going to restore healthcare to U.S. citizens. In fact, since Medicaid cuts are helping to fund this ICE crackdown, it’s doing the opposite. Meanwhile, the extremely wealthy Americans who got their taxes cut by the same law can afford gold-plated health plans. Addressing this country’s health inequities means closing our massive wealth gap, not scapegoating immigrants. There must be higher taxation on the wealthy so we can restore and expand health programs like Medicaid and Medicare. Healthcare is a human right, rooted in the belief that every person deserves dignity and care, regardless of where they were born or what job they work. We must hold accountable those who promote harmful rhetoric that justifies the exclusion of immigrants, which ultimately only hurts all of us. This op-ed was distributed via Oth​er​Words​.org.

articles.title: The Rising Left Can’t Ignore Labor’s Ongoing Crisis
articles.author: Sam Gindin
articles.content: As the Trump administration stumbles from scandal to scandal and worries over artificial intelligence reach a fever pitch, there seems to be little relief in sight for working-class Americans confronting a stubborn cost-of-living crisis. The failure of both Republicans and Democrats to advance real solutions to the affordability crunch has opened the door to hopeful socialist election victories, including Zohran Mamdani’s triumph in New York last year and several left-wing wins in congressional primaries this summer. Yet organized labor by and large has continued its long retreat, and the prospects of significant national policy change still look remote. Sam Gindin is one of the most exacting and capacious thinkers on the socialist left today. With decades of experience in the labor movement as research director for the Canadian Auto Workers (which merged in 2013 with the Communications, Energy, and Paperworkers Union to form Unifor, today the largest private sector union in Canada), his political orientation is grounded in the reality of the contemporary state of organized labor. His perspective is also informed by a careful study of the current political-economic conjuncture, evident most notably in his important work with Leo Panitch, The Making of Global Capitalism . Damage magazine editor and frequent Jacobin contributor Benjamin Y. Fong recently interviewed Gindin about the current political moment. They discussed the contemporary crisis of capitalism, the privileged position of organized labor among social movements, and the crucial importance of organizing Amazon today. Benjamin Y. Fong How do you understand the contemporary crisis of capitalism? And what do you mean when you say you oppose “crisis-mongering as politics”? Sam Gindin There is a crisis today of the legitimacy of political institutions and a crisis for working families, but not a crisis of American economic decline. People are suffering and insecure, but the US economy is growing, the share of profits is at record levels, overall investment is growing, albeit unevenly, and technology and productivity are advancing. There are conflicts with China, but China has neither the interest nor capacity to take over America’s international role. People are frustrated and angry over what the successes of capitalism have wrought but unable to convert the political delegitimation of the United States into a crisis of capitalism. So it’s not a crisis of capitalism but really a crisis of the labor movement and the Left. Crisis-mongering subordinates serious economic and political analysis to exaggerated warnings of imminent collapse. The hope is that this will spur people into action. It looks to decline to do the heavy lifting for us. This betrays the actual challenges we face and the need for the kind of deep and long-term organizing we actually need. It also fails even as a populist mobilizing tactic; it could just as easily make people feel like, “Well, what’s the point? The world’s going to come to an end soon.” In the end, it undermines the credibility of the Left in repeatedly presenting overblown declarations that don’t come to pass. Benjamin Y. Fong The Left today is very electorally focused, and from one angle, that’s a direct way of intervening in this crisis of legitimacy. But from another, you could see this electoralism without first rebuilding the base as a kind of quick fix too. Sam Gindin Absolutely. Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani deserve credit for affecting political discourse, generating enthusiasm among young people and moving them from protest to politics. But there is a limit to even “left-ish” politics if there is no solid base on the ground. And while social democratic politics can have some impact on that base, the electoral arena is not conducive to building its depth. Elections look for numbers, not the quality of understanding and commitment. They tend to be about quick, door-step exchanges, not the genuine conversations that organizing entails. They also tend to cater to where the polls tell us people are (generally some middle ground) and not to what it might take to change people. It’s the building of a genuine base for social transformation that ultimately makes elections relevant; elections by themselves don’t build the base. Socialism will come from many streams, and whatever helps is welcome. But what’s needed is not just adding up various movements or making social democrats “better.” We need an appreciation of how profound transforming capitalism is, and we also need an organized orientation to building the kind of social force that can eventually replace it. This is especially so because of a polarization of options today. Decades of capitalist restructuring of workplaces, industries, and communities; of globalization, financialization, and neoliberalism — all alongside the stagnation of labor and the Left — have negated middle of the road responses. Capital and the state have made significant reforms near impossible (“There Is No Alternative”), and in this context, radical politics tends to be the only practical politics. The Place of Labor Benjamin Y. Fong André Gorz once said that the success or failure of a wide variety of progressive causes, from gender equality to immigrant rights, will largely depend on that of the trade union movement. Why does organized labor hold a privileged position here? Sam Gindin About a dozen years before he said this, Gorz’s book, Farewell to the Working Class , seemed to write off the radical potential of workers. What you’re referencing is his later, changed view, in which he came to realize that most movements simply can’t — unlike labor — sustain themselves over time. For all the weakness of the American labor movement in the United States, it still has some $35 billion in assets and 14 million unionized members. Most movements don’t have those kinds of resources, and they regularly look to unions for financial assistance. In saying this, we should not separate unions from movements that address social needs. Workers obviously have lives outside the workplace and care very much about universal healthcare, affordable shelter, adequate transportation, the environment their kids face, etc. What working-class organizations offer is not just financial resources. They also play a role in uniting the interests of workers as workers and in organizing working people as part of society more broadly. Benjamin Y. Fong Many would characterize the key issue here as one of restoring labor’s militancy. Is that the key problem? Sam Gindin In the absence of resistance/militancy, the conditions of workers can’t be advanced. So yes, restoring militancy is fundamental. But it’s not enough to have militancy, and this was graphically demonstrated in the 1960s. When the postwar boom ended, workers stubbornly resisted lowering their monetary expectations and the unilateral authority of managers. This blocked the restoration of the status quo at their expense and was a factor in the downturn of profits and the rise of inflation, both of which threatened the status of the US dollar. The labor movement hung on for nearly a decade after that, but without going beyond workplace-by-workplace militancy to broader politicization along class lines, including demanding the democratization of investment decisions and guaranteed full employment, labor’s ultimate defeat was preordained. The eventual response from the state was an engineered recession (near-20-percent interest rates) that weakened and exhausted the unions. Neoliberalism arrived. Capital’s crisis was solved by way of a greater and longer-lasting crisis for the working class. The message of the ’60s is therefore that workplace militancy is essential but not enough. Benjamin Y. Fong You also emphasize the importance of socialist organization outside of unions. Sam Gindin Absolutely. The kind of politicization I raised above is unlikely without the role of organized socialists with one foot in the workplace and unions and one outside. Unions are particularist organizations, not class organizations: they represent a particular group of workers that happen to be working together. The role of organized socialists is to overcome the fragmentation of workers across workplaces, unions, economic sectors, and communities. It’s also to overcome the separation of individual workers from other dimensions of their lives. This is all the more important today. In the 1950s and ’60s, unionized workers in auto and steel could win a great deal on their own, but that period is largely over. Given capital’s increased power since then, workers can’t win without thinking in larger terms, i.e., in terms of the class as a whole. That means making connections across workplaces, sectors, and communities. Unions are limited in doing this, and that’s where socialist organizations come in. Building the class into a coherent social force is (or should be) their prime focus. I’m not making an ideological point. It’s a practical issue to be clear about who your enemy is. Employers are the face of the enemy, but they are not the enemy. What constrains improvement in working conditions is the threat of competition. Employers defend the pressure they put on workers with the claim that competition forces them to do so to survive. Moreover, competition is asymmetrical. As stronger capitalists devour weaker ones, capital becomes stronger as a class. However, for workers, competition undermines their primary strength — solidarity — and so weakens them. It’s important to raise these points in educational meetings organized by or outside the union. Some people think of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) as the place to do this. But DSA is also really fractured. Benjamin Y. Fong It could be that the very fragmentation of DSA is a kind of virtue right now. I don’t think it’ll ever be the party organization that some people hope it will be, but it’s a place to meet people. Sam Gindin I think that’s true. There seem to be distinct groups which are in essence mini-parties — each has their own analysis, do their own education, take specific positions. Under the banner of DSA, they meet, discuss, and debate strategy. That’s important because premature mergers, even among socialists, can paper over differences, and then the organization disintegrates. But from afar, I don’t know how sharp the debates are. Sometimes, in the name of unity, the more difficult debates are avoided, but such debates are important for mutual development. It does seem that certain crucial issues like how to relate to the Democratic Party, and at what scale (local/municipal, state, national) electoral contestation should take place, are coming to a head. Splits are likely necessary, but they can be very destructive. It’s worth it, in this context, to examine how Syriza and Momentum went from glory to obliteration, but there’s been too little of such investigations on the Left. The Amazon Project Benjamin Y. Fong You’ve said that unions need a “virtual crusade” to make a dramatic leap forward. Why is that the case, and is the struggle to organize Amazon that crusade? Sam Gindin In the 1930s, the Congress of Industrial Organizations sparked a breakthrough in industrial unionism. John Lewis of the United Mine Workers grasped that if steel wasn’t also unionized, the miners would be isolated. So he sent one hundred of his organizers out to support the organizing of the steel industry. That kind of sensibility is especially pertinent today given the expanding imbalance of power between capital and labor, the result of massive economic, social, and political changes over decades that can’t be addressed with marginal tactical changes. This imbalance demands the kind of leap forward that brings submerged frustrations to life and transforms working-class expectations, institutional capacities, and confidence. This amounts to a crusade, both organizationally and culturally. There are any number of struggles that could act as the catalyst for such a crusade. Amazon is only one such catalyst-in-waiting, but Amazon’s iconic status — the largest private sector employer in the United States, a leader in high tech and artificial intelligence that links some two million businesses with some 300 million consumers — would make its unionization the most important breakthrough in generations. The labor movement has, however, already lost a step in approaching Amazon as a pie to be split between different unions — warehouses for the Teamsters, Whole Foods for the United Food and Commercial Workers — rather than as a project for the whole labor movement. The catch, of course, is that labor’s extended stagnation has profoundly weakened the very capacities needed to rethink and transform it. It’s still possible for Amazon workers to win significant footholds, and if Amazon continues to stonewall, as it obviously will, then the challenge to the labor movement as a whole will become more pressing. The key test will not only lie in whether labor provides the needed financial support at the requisite moment, but also in the readiness of already unionized workers to disrupt Amazon as needed at ports, in rail and trucking, and in parcel delivery. Benjamin Y. Fong Tactically, there’s a lot of emphasis today on salting, or taking a job at Amazon and organizing it from the inside. What do you make of this? Sam Gindin Salts are critical. Organizing from a base within the workplace is the most successful way to develop relationships with workers, and also to talk to workers about issues beyond the workplace. But salts also need a supportive structure outside the workplace: trained organizers to follow up on contacts, leaflet, generate support for the struggle across Amazon facilities that don’t yet have salts. They also need resources for meeting spaces, socials, sustaining workers laid off or fired, etc. This demands a union that has your back: an institution that can help strengthen confidence and provide staying power among both the organizers and the workers. Benjamin Y. Fong Could you say a bit more about how you situate the Amazon organizing project in the present crisis of labor? Sam Gindin Amazon has the possibility of being a spur to the revival of the labor movement. What will labor’s role be in this present conjuncture, in the crisis of legitimacy? Amazon is the test that helps us answer this broader question. Will labor stand up to this challenge, which has the potential to revive the movement, or will it remain too particularist to take advantage of it? Contrary to what many union leaders and also many on the Left assert, the labor movement is not — in spite of some impressive and courageous struggles — about to “turn the corner” and become a powerful social force again. Some union supporters reject such assessments as counterproductive; what workers need, they say, is inspiration. However being sober about where things are at is never counterproductive. Inspiration is great, but if it isn’t based on concrete achievements, it ends up as a rhetorical substitute for actual organizing. It’s an interesting moment in terms of language. A lot of language that used to distinguish us is now common language. So when you say we need class formation, everybody nods their heads. We say you have to think in class terms, they nod their heads. When you say that social democracy is limited, they nod their heads. But do they really understand the inevitable rupture when it comes time to govern? If they did, they’d understand that we’re going to need a really deep base. That we’re going to need allies, and that nothing will be easy. So the Amazon organizing project could also be a way of injecting some reality back into conversations about what it means to reckon with the present crisis. Benjamin Y. Fong What would winning the fight at Amazon mean? Sam Gindin A specific aspect of Amazon’s model is that it is regionally rooted. Its massive facilities are concentrated at ports and key transportation hubs, with some regions being of much more strategic importance than others. This regional rootedness means that establishing leverage does not have to wait until all of Amazon is unionized; a strategic number of unionized regional facilities can be effective. Within regions, the company’s fulfillment centers (FCs) are critical. From the perspective of class formation, that’s where most of the workers are. For the company to move these facilities to avoid unions would be difficult, given the high investment costs of FCs. Amazon’s determined resistance to avoid unions demands a revisiting of tactics that have largely been mothballed by organized labor over the years, and at great cost to their dynamism. Their successful rediscovery, along with other creative organizing innovations, is so vital because they can potentially have explosive implications beyond Amazon, challenging union approaches throughout the labor movement. Unannounced disruptive tactics carry a special weight. With Amazon’s powerful logistics network, the traditional strike deadlines declared in advance won’t work. Given advance warning, Amazon would simply reorganize its distribution network to neutralize a dated work stoppage. Disciplined, creative, and sporadic disruption are therefore key for workers. The labor movement was born out of work disruptions (sit-downs, wildcats, health and safety refusals, rejection of production speed-ups), but its trajectory has moved away from those earlier tactics. The revival of the tactic of unannounced disruptions is inseparable from the revival of the labor movement. To take advantage of it, it is also crucial to establish a strong everyday workplace presence, one based on prioritizing work standards, health and safety, and interventions in management authority. This in turn requires not only union majorities but large majorities and deep commitments; a simple majority of union cards is not enough. Benjamin Y. Fong Are you optimistic looking ahead? Sam Gindin Yes, but soberly so. It’s a really difficult thing to commit to and believe in socialism, but there’s no other option. Is this just pie in the sky? I can see someone doing the same analysis as me and writing it off. The chances of it being pulled off are one in one thousand. And I might not disagree about the odds and all the limits. But my response is, “Well, actually, one in one thousand is pretty good. We’ll take those odds.” What else are you going to do with your life?
